blocks.text: A **linked list** is a chain of small boxes called **nodes**. Each node holds two things: a **value**, and an **arrow** (a pointer) to the next node. You hold on to the first node — the **head** — and follow the arrows to reach everything else. The last node's arrow points to **null**, which means "the list ends here".

blocks.alt: A linked list of four nodes holding 10, 20, 30 and 40. Each node has a value part and a next part. The head label points at 10, each next arrow points to the following node, and the last node points to null.
blocks.caption: One node = one value + one arrow to the next node.

blocks.text: In a treasure hunt, each clue tells you **where the next clue is hidden**. You can't jump to clue number 4 — you have to start at clue 1 and follow the trail. A linked list works exactly the same way:

items: Each **node** is a clue: it has some information (the value) and directions to the next clue (the `next` pointer).
The **head** is the first clue — the only one you're handed directly.
**null** is the last clue saying "this is the end, there is no next".

blocks.text: An array keeps its elements **side by side** in one block of memory. A linked list doesn't: each node is created on its own, wherever the computer finds free space. The arrows are what hold the list together — each `next` stores the **memory address** of the following node.

blocks.alt: Top: an array of 10, 20, 30, 40 stored in four neighbouring memory slots. Bottom: the same values as linked list nodes scattered around memory at addresses 0x7a10, 0x3c40, 0x9e08 and 0x5b20, joined by arrows that store those addresses.
blocks.caption: Nodes live wherever there was room. Only the arrows connect them.

blocks.text: That one difference explains almost everything about linked lists: why adding a node is cheap (just create it anywhere and change an arrow), and why reaching the 500th node is slow (you must follow 500 arrows to get there).
A node is a tiny class with two fields. This is exactly how LeetCode and most interview questions define it:
Building the list from the picture above means creating four nodes and connecting their arrows:

blocks.code:
head = ListNode(10)
head.next = ListNode(20)
head.next.next = ListNode(30)
head.next.next.next = ListNode(40)   # 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40 -> None

blocks.text: Because we only hold the head, every operation starts the same way: put a pointer `curr` on the head, and keep moving it with `curr = curr.next` until it becomes null. This is called **traversing** the list.

blocks.caption: Watch curr hop from node to node. It can only ever move forward, one arrow at a time.

blocks.alt: A glossary drawing: head is the first node, tail is the last node, next is the arrow to the following node, and null marks the end. Node 10 is labelled head and node 30 tail.

null   "no node here" - the end of the list

blocks.text: The three types of linked list
Every linked list is nodes joined by arrows. The **three types** differ in which arrows each node has, and where the last one points. This course covers all three:

items: **Singly linked** — each node has one arrow, `next`. You can only move forward, and the list ends at **null**. The type interviews use most.
**Doubly linked** — each node also has a `prev` arrow back to the node before it, so you can walk **both ways** and remove a node without searching for its neighbour.
**Circular** — the last node points **back to the first** instead of to null, so the list has no end: walking it goes round and round.

blocks.alt: Three small diagrams. Singly linked: arrows only go forward. Doubly linked: each node has arrows forward and backward. Circular: the last node points back to the first instead of null.

elements.text: the tail points back to the head

blocks.text: The next lesson looks at each type in detail: its node in code, what it costs, and when to pick it. Later lessons show how to **traverse**, insert and delete in all three, and the interview questions are grouped by type.

items: A linked list is a chain of **nodes**; each node stores a **value** and a **next** pointer.
You only hold the **head**. Everything else is reached by following arrows.
Nodes are scattered in memory — the arrows, not positions, define the order.
The last node points to **null**. Checking for null is how every loop knows when to stop.
There are **three types**: **singly** (next only), **doubly** (prev and next) and **circular** (the last node points back to the first).
